1:
Four commentators agree the chapter division is wrong and the first verse belongs with the discourse before it, and then divide sharply over what it promises. Robertson lays the problem out without settling it, noting that Luke has them see the kingdom of God, Matthew the Son of man coming as a process, and Mark the kingdom already come and with power; he observes that the second advent plainly did not occur while any of those standing there lived, and canvasses the transfiguration that follows immediately, the descent of the Spirit at Pentecost, and the destruction of the temple, leaving open whether the same event is meant here as in the verse before. Ellicott presses the tense, that they should see it not coming but as having actually come in its completeness. Lightfoot takes the whole phrase as the standing idiom for vengeance on the Jewish nation and lists six scriptural forms of it, the great and terrible day, the end of the world, the last times, the new world, the coming in the clouds, the enthroning of the apostles. Henry combines that with the conquest of Gentile idolatry. Wesley dates it simply to Pentecost, when three thousand were converted at once.

Lightfoot opens his note on the mountain by asking the reader's pardon, since he knows it will be laughed at to doubt that the transfiguration happened on Tabor, and then lays out his reasons: the previous story leaves Jesus in the coasts of Caesarea Philippi with no change of place recorded, the evangelists mention no journey but only the leading up of three disciples, and it would be strange to tire himself with so long a march to a mountain he had never used when there were mountains where he commonly resorted. Clarke reports the same conjecture and prefers it to both Tabor and Hermon; Robertson takes Hermon for granted and suggests its snow-capped summit was visible that very night. On the raiment Barnes corrects the English, since the man in question was a scourer whose office was to whiten cloth rather than a fuller who thickened it; Ellicott notes the words as snow are wanting in the best manuscripts and calls the comparison with clothes fresh from the bleacher's hands peculiar to this evangelist in its homely vividness. Robertson explains Peter's remark charitably, that he may have been embarrassed at having been asleep and that the feast of booths was near.

Two reconstructions compete for what the disciples were really asking on the way down. Chrysostom puts the argument in their mouths: we have seen Elias with thee, and we saw thee before we saw Elias, but the scribes say Elias comes first, so we conclude they have lied. The answer he finds in the reply is a distinction of two advents, Elias being forerunner of the second as John was of the first. Bede offers another: they took the change they had seen on the mountain for the coming in glory itself, and asked why the forerunner had not appeared, particularly as they had just watched Elias depart; he adds that the restoring of all things is what Malachi foretold, and that Elias when he comes must also pay the debt of death his prolonged life has deferred. Origen keeps to the plain reason for the silence, that the mystery was not to be published before the glory of the passion and resurrection. Robertson observes that the phrase about rising from the dead had escaped them earlier and now catches their attention, and that the master patiently enlightens dull pupils arguing over the exegesis of the scribes. Clarke notes that the tenth verse is absent from two manuscripts.
14:
Calvin opens on the puzzle of the tone. A father pleads for an only son, the need is urgent, the appeal modest, and yet the answer breaks out in a severity quite unlike the gentleness with which even importunate requests were usually met; and because the other two evangelists give no reason for it, some interpreters have wrongly aimed the rebuke at the disciples or at the father. Chrysostom locates the fault in the father, who prays in the middle of a crowd while accusing the disciples, and is answered before the same crowd by a charge extended to the whole nation. Bede reads the scene from the other side, observing that the scribes are nowhere credited with devotion or reverence while the multitude was amazed and ran and saluted, and reconstructing the question under dispute as being simply why the disciples could not heal the boy. Robertson says the same more bluntly, that it was like the professional scribes to take a keen interest in the failure of the nine and to nag and quiz them, and that the party from the mountain arrived to find them at it. Barnes notes the debate had been got up in the master's absence.

The clinical detail is the feature everyone marks as peculiar to this Gospel. Ellicott lists what only Mark supplies: the amazement of the crowd, the dumb spirit, the gnashing of the teeth, the pining away, the falling and wallowing, the question about how long it had lasted, the fire and the water. Robertson works through the verbs one by one, the word for seizing which gives us catalepsy and which the old physicians used of fits, the word for dashing down, the poetic word for foaming, the word for a shrill squeak, the word for drying up like grass. Calvin declines to make the case merely natural or merely demonic: the term used elsewhere belongs to those seized with epilepsy at the waning of the moon, and he refuses Chrysostom's suggestion that the word was a trick of Satan to disgrace the creatures of God, since experience shows the course of the moon does affect such diseases; his conclusion is that Satan had taken the tongue and ears while availing himself of a weakness of brain and nerves already there. Clarke draws the opposite inference from the address to the spirit, that a natural disease could not properly be commanded to come out and enter no more.

On the exchange of conditions Robertson notes the Greek turns the father's own words back on him by making them the subject of the sentence, so that the challenge runs: as to your if thou canst, all things are possible to the believer. Calvin draws the doctrine out, that it is not the Lord who prevents his benefits from flowing in abundance but the narrowness of our faith that lets them come only in drops, and warns against the idle ingenuity that would make the saying prove a man can believe of himself. Clarke turns it on the reader, asking why our own souls are not wholly healed and answering that Jesus is able and willing but we are not willing to give up our idols. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts omit the word believe, leaving a sadder reading in which the master simply repeats the father's half-despairing phrase. Two other short readings go the same way: the tears in the next verse and the fasting at the close are both absent from the oldest witnesses. Robertson takes the second omission further, holding the addition needless and untrue, since the nine were powerless because they were prayerless and their self-complacency spelled defeat.
30:
Two explanations are given for the privacy of the journey through Galilee. Henry makes it a judgment, that having done many mighty works among them in vain he would not invite them to see more, and turns instead to the disciples, who needed preparing for the trial ahead. Robertson makes it strategic and rather bleak, that he was back in Galilee but avoiding public work there, no longer the hero of the province. Wesley combines the two, that they went by the cities rather than through them, along the most private ways, because he wanted time alone with the twelve. On the failure to understand, Bede argues the ignorance came not so much from slowness of intellect as from love, since being still carnal and unacquainted with the mystery of the cross they could not believe that one they had recognised as God was about to die, and being used to figurative speech they took the plain words for another figure. Robertson notes the imperfect tense, that they continued not to understand, and suggests they were afraid to ask because of the bitter memory of the name flung at Peter when he protested last time. Clarke reports that the whole verse is missing from two manuscripts.

Bede offers a cause for the quarrel about precedence that the text does not supply: three of them had been taken apart into the mountain and entrusted with something secret, and the keys had been promised to one of those three, which was enough to set the rest disputing. Chrysostom is occupied instead with harmonising the accounts, since one evangelist has the disciples come and ask who is greatest while here the question is put to them; his answer is either that the other writer began further on, omitting the master's knowledge of their thoughts, or else that what they thought and said away from him was as good as said to him, being equally known. Robertson reads the scene psychologically, that the dispute was not about the coming death but about relative rank in the political kingdom they still expected, that the question had probably been raised first by them and then pressed further to reach the heated argument on the road, and that their silence was the shame of being found out. Clarke identifies the house as Peter's, where he ordinarily lodged; Robertson adds that the child called in may well have been Peter's own.

The answer is given deliberately and in a fixed form. Robertson marks the sitting down as a considered way of handling a delicate situation and states the rule as a straight inversion, that whoever would be first shall be last of all and servant of all, a saying repeated on other occasions. On the gesture Ellicott notes that the Greek uses a single participle found only here and in one later chapter, and that it more probably means the arms were folded round the child than that the child was lifted up. Gill guards the application from being taken literally, since the promise cannot be about picking up infants but about showing the least kindness to the meanest believer who resembles a child in humility and lowliness, and he cites the versions that render it one like to this child. Ellicott traces the ladder the saying climbs, from receiving a child for Christ's sake to receiving Christ and so entering fellowship with the Father. Robertson observes bluntly that the lesson did not take, since the twelve wrangle over primacy again two chapters later and still fail to understand his attitude to children.
38:
Who the unlicensed exorcist was is answered by conjecture, and the conjectures converge. Barnes suggests one of the Baptist's disciples or one of the seventy, and denies there is any evidence he was a mere exorcist using the name as a pretence. Clarke reasons that a man who knew nothing of Christ could scarcely work a miracle in his name, and settles on the same two possibilities, adding that one of the seventy might have left the company after his commission while keeping his faith and so keeping the power. Lightfoot builds the fullest reconstruction: the man truly cast out devils and by divine power, or the reply would not have been what it was; he cast them out in the name of Messiah rather than of Jesus; and his not following was ignorance rather than contempt, since he had probably been baptized by John into the name of a Messiah shortly to come without yet knowing that Jesus of Nazareth was he. Calvin is more suspicious, allowing that the man may have acted with no bad intention but judging that he had seized an office never given him, while granting that God is sometimes pleased to throw lustre round his name by ministries he does not approve as lawful.

On the motive of the objection the readings differ. Chrysostom clears the disciple of jealousy or envy, holding that he wished everyone who called on the name to follow and be one body with the rest, and that many believers received gifts without being with Christ, some pure in life but imperfect in faith and others the reverse. Bede has him loving with eminent devotion and concluding that a man performing an office he had no right to should be shut out from its benefit, against which the reply establishes that nobody is to be driven away from the partial goodness he already has but rather stirred up toward what he has not yet reached. Ellicott finds the same zeal that later wanted fire called down on a Samaritan village, and reads the remark as self-vindication, a claim to have received the master and refused to receive anyone who did not openly follow him. Robertson is least generous, suggesting the story was told to change an embarrassing subject and in expectation of praise, and that the preceding saying may have raised a doubt in the speaker's mind about his own narrowness. Wesley simply asks how often the same temper is found in ourselves.

The maxim about not being against us looks like the flat contradiction of another saying, and Augustine takes the difficulty head on, considering and rejecting the escape that one saying concerns the disciples and the other Christ himself, since a man joined to the disciples as members cannot fail to be with the head; his answer is that a man is not with him precisely so far as he is against him. Wesley reaches a similar reconciliation by purpose rather than logic, that the one proverb warns hearers no neutrality is possible in the war with Satan while the other directs his followers to judge men candidly, so that we are to be rigorous in judging ourselves and candid in judging each other. Clarke prefers the reading not against you and points to the parallel where Joshua asked Moses to forbid two men prophesying in the camp; Ellicott cites the same episode and adds the later rejoicing that Christ was preached every way. Calvin guards the concession, that this is no licence for rash men to disturb the order of the church, and that such people are not thereby acknowledged as disciples, only reckoned useful so far as they do no harm.
42:
The hand, foot and eye are read by the older commentators as people rather than parts. Chrysostom states it flatly, that this is said not of our limbs but of our intimate friends, whom we look on as limbs because we need them, since nothing is so hurtful as mischievous society. Bede develops the same reading at length, taking the hand for the close friend whose help we daily require, and concluding that such a man must be driven from our company if he would hurt us in what concerns the soul, lest by choosing a portion in this life with one who is lost we perish with him in the next. Wesley agrees and marks the transition, that the discourse has moved from the case of giving offence to that of taking it, so that the saying relates primarily to persons and only secondarily to things. Gill keeps the wider sense of parting with whatever is nearest, and supplies the rabbinic background: the Jewish canons prescribed cutting off the hand in certain cases, language never meant for execution but framed to show the heinousness of the crime and deter men from it. Lightfoot quotes the rabbinic text itself.

The refrain about the worm and the fire raises a textual question and a topographical one. Robertson reports that the oldest and best manuscripts lack two of the three occurrences, which came in from later families as a mere repetition of the third, and that this is why two verse numbers are missing from the modern text; Clarke had already noted the clause about unquenchable fire absent from several witnesses at both places. On the source all agree: the words come almost verbatim from the last verse of Isaiah, where the worshippers go out to look on the carcases of the transgressors, and both Barnes and Ellicott trace the imagery to a battlefield, the worm feeding while there are bodies to devour and the fire burning until they are consumed. Where they part is over the valley. Robertson states as fact that the Valley of Hinnom, desecrated by the sacrifice of children, was used for the city garbage where worms gnawed and fires burned. Ellicott allows it as a possibility, that the valley may have received the solid as well as the fluid sewage of the city and so become a visible type, but warns that the authorities are hardly definite enough to warrant the positive statement.

Whether either image is literal is disputed across the whole range. Chrysostom denies a visible worm and identifies it with conscience gnawing the soul for the good it has not done, so that each man is made his own accuser by remembering what he did in this mortal life. Gill takes the same line and presses it into detail, conscience flying in the sinner's face, accusing, upbraiding, aggravating, never ceasing; Wesley names the particular gnawings, pride, self-will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow and despair. Barnes goes furthest, supposing no real worm and perhaps no material fire, and treating the whole as a figure for destruction that is awful, wide-spread and eternal. Augustine works through the question more carefully than any of them, reporting those who assign both worm and fire to the soul and read the fire as burning grief, on the strength of the apostle asking who is offended and he burns not; he judges it more credible that there will be pain of body and of soul alike, and concludes that it is easier to say both belong to the body than that neither does. Bede takes the middle course, the worm accusing inwardly and the fire raging without.
49:
Barnes opens by conceding that perhaps no passage in the New Testament has given commentators more perplexity, and that it may now be impossible to fix its precise meaning. The manuscripts are part of the trouble. Ellicott reports that many of the best copies omit the second clause while one of the best omits the first, as though transcribers felt either clause more intelligible alone than the two together; Clarke names the Codex Bezae for the first omission and notes other copies dropping the last. Scaliger cut the knot by emending the text to read that every sacrifice of flour shall be salted, and both Clarke and Lightfoot refuse him, Clarke calling the change taking the text by storm and Lightfoot reporting that the great Scaliger was well chastised for it, and not without cause, by John Cloppenberg. Lightfoot's own solution keeps the received words and restricts their subject: every one means not every man but every one of those whose worm dieth not, and the sense is that they shall be seasoned with fire so as to become unconsumable and endure for ever to be tormented, as salt preserves flesh from corruption. He supports it from Jewish comment on the same verse of Isaiah.

Gill takes the same road as Lightfoot, that the fire will be to the damned what salt is to flesh, preserving them in their beings so that they are tormented without being consumed. Ellicott sets out three objections to exactly this reading: it arbitrarily narrows the every one of the sentence to the finally condemned; it is scarcely conceivable that the one word salted should carry contrasted senses within a single verse; and it runs against the uniform symbolism of salt elsewhere, which stands for what purifies and preserves from taint. Calvin takes the sacrificial sense instead, that believers are exhorted to offer themselves now to be seasoned and made devoted offerings, on the model of the law requiring every meat offering to be salted, and holds that they are salted by the word of the gospel. Barnes goes further and suspects the verse has no reference to future punishment at all, the difficulty having arisen from reading it as a reason for what precedes rather than as part of the chapter's main argument about tolerance. Wesley refuses to choose and takes both, the man who will not part with hand or eye salted with a fire that preserves, the willing sacrifice salted with grace.

On the closing words Ellicott marks a difference from the parallel in the first Gospel, where the salt is the visible community preserving the world, whereas here it is the inward grace that alone makes the community what it should be. He also supplies the link that ties the end of the chapter to its middle, since the injunction to have peace looks back to the dispute on the road about who was greatest, purity from selfish aims being the chief preservative of peace. Barnes and Clarke read the connection the same way, Barnes glossing it as an end to struggling for places and honours, Clarke as a proof of freedom from ambition that will satisfy their own minds and silence the world. Robertson dwells on the alternative, that salt which has gone flat cannot be seasoned by anything and is fit to season nothing, an exploded shell, a burnt-out crater, a spent force. Calvin weighs two senses for the word here and prefers the one that continues the previous discourse, exhorting them to keep the rigour of faith so as to purify others; but he adds a caution, that since salt bites by its sharpness the seasoning must be regulated so that peace is preserved entire.
